title: Earth Curvature Calculator: The Drop, Computed
description: Calculate how far the Earth's surface drops over any distance with the Earth Curvature Calculator — spherical geometry, no refraction. Free.
summary_sentence: For example, over 10 miles the surface drops 20.3 metres (about 67 feet) below a level tangent — the famous '8 inches per mile squared' rule, computed exactly.
quick_answer: The Earth Curvature Calculator computes how far the Earth's surface falls below a horizontal tangent over a given distance, on a spherical Earth. Enter the distance and read the drop in metres, feet or inches — the geometry behind horizon dip, long sight lines and a century of shoreline demonstrations.

body.t: A lighthouse, a skyline, a wind farm across the water: the drop over the intervening distance is the first term in whether it can show. The
finishes the argument with your eye height added.

Chicago's skyline from the Michigan shore is about 53 miles — at that range the drop is roughly 570 m of geometry that refraction and tower height then negotiate with. Compute the drop first; argue about the rest second.
Precise levelling corrects for curvature run by run (about 0.08 m at 1 km) — this page is that correction, generalised to any distance.
Long-lens photos across bays invite curvature claims in both directions. The drop over the photo's distance is a five-second calculation that settles the geometry half of the argument.

The old rule says drop ≈ 8 inches × (miles)². Exact spherical geometry at 1 mile gives 0.203 m — 8.0 inches. At 10 miles the rule predicts 800 inches (20.3 m) and geometry agrees to the centimetre. A rare folk formula that survives audit.
At 10 km the drop is 7.85 m — a two-storey building's worth. Anything shorter than that at 10 km, viewed from ground level with no refraction, is below the tangent line's world entirely.

popular_table.title: Curvature drop by distance (spherical, no refraction)
popular_table.intro: Computed as R(sec(d/R) − 1) — the calculator's own formula.
popular_table.note: Drop grows with the square of distance (the d²⁄2R approximation is within a percent out to ~100 km). Refraction bends light downward and reduces the effective drop — typically by roughly a seventh under standard conditions.

faq: What is the difference between drop and bulge?

Drop is measured from a tangent at one point (surveyor's view); bulge is the surface rising toward a chord between two points (link planner's view). Same circle, different ruler — at equal distances, tangent drop is four times the midpoint bulge.
Why do photos sometimes show more than the drop allows?

Refraction: temperature layers bend light, sometimes strongly (superior mirage conditions can lift distant objects dramatically). The geometric drop is the baseline; the atmosphere argues from there, in both directions.
Does my height change the drop?
The drop is a property of the surface alone. Your height changes what you can see over it — that is the horizon distance and hidden height calculation, the companion pages to this one.
For distances up to a few hundred kilometres, yes — its error stays under 1%. The calculator uses the exact circular form anyway, so the question is academic here.

Local curvature varies slightly with latitude and direction (the Earth's radius of curvature runs about 6,357–6,399 km). At 100 km that shifts the drop by well under a metre — stated for completeness, invisible to most uses.
Not with the naked eye at short range (0.08 m over 1 km hides below waves and haze) — which is exactly why instruments, not impressions, settled the question centuries ago.
How does this relate to the horizon dip angle?

The dip is the angular version: at eye level the horizon sits below horizontal by an angle that grows with your height — computed on the Horizon Distance page. Drop is distance's version of the same circle.
